newsitem.title: RUSSIA: "I have nothing to hide," Yeltsin tells Russians. [CORRECTED 19:18 GMT]
newsitem.headline: "I have nothing to hide," Yeltsin tells Russians. [CORRECTED 19:18 GMT]

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, after breaking weeks of near total silence to reveal that he will undergo heart surgery, says in a magazine interview to be published on Monday that he has nothing to hide from the nation.
The magazine, Itogi, has also unearthed what it calls the dramatic inside story of how Yeltsin first refused and was then persuaded to have the operation.
Editor Sergei Parkhomenko told Reuters that he thought Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin was the man who changed Yeltsin's mind.
Chernomyrdin is the only leader to have visited Yeltsin since he went to his Rus residence outside Moscow on August 26 for a holiday.
"He must have told Yeltsin -- look, the same surgeon did the same operation on me in 1992 and here I am, alive and fit," Parkhomenko said.
Parkhomenko said he started digging into the question of Yeltsin's health last month and found several cardiologists ready to discuss "this complicated medical case".

Moscow's Cardiological Centre, headed by top heart specialist Yevgeny Chazov, conducted "coronorography" tests on the president in mid-August which showed the need for an operation on the blood vessels supplying his heart. Chazov confirmed this on Friday to Interfax news agency.
And then the probelms began, Parkhomenko said. Yeltsin refused.
Several doctors told Parkhomenko such behaviour was typical for many patients, especially those in responsible posts with a strong will and a desire to lead.

"Nothing harms a patient more than the oppressive feeling that illness is a sign of weakness, as if it is something shameful, as if the patient is to blame," Parkhomenko's article quotes an experienced doctor as saying.
Moreover, most of the best Russian heart surgeons refused to consider operating on the 65-year-old president, fearing failure, Parkhomenko told Reuters (corrects age from 85).
But one, Professor Rinat Akchurin, the chief surgeon at Chazov's centre, said: "I will do it, I did the same for Chernomyrdin in 1992".
There was no independent confirmation of Chernomyrdin's operation. But Chazov told Interfax that if the president chose his centre the operation would be performed by Akchurin.

Official reports said Yeltsin and Chernomyrdin discussed state affairs during a long meeting at the Rus residence last Monday, but Parkhomenko said it was then that Chernomyrdin apparently persuaded the president to undergo the surgery.
Yeltsin announced his decision in a television interview on Thursday, saying he had opted for an operation because doctors promised he would have an active life.
The text of his written interview with Itogi, received by the magazine a day before the announcement, seemed to show that he had made up his mind by then.

"The times when the top leader appeared once a year, somewhere atop the mausoleum, and the country was in fact ruled by a faceless crowd of bureaucrats, are in the past along with the communist regime and, I am convinced, will never return," Yeltsin said.
Soviet leaders traditionally appeared on top of Soviet founding father Vladimir Lenin's mausoleum on Red Square during annual public parades.
"It is the duty of the president to make sure that every voter is convinced that the country is in reliable and firm hands, the very same hands into which he put it by voting," Yeltsin said.
"That is why I deem it necessary to talk to the Russians openly and calmly. I have nothing to hide from them."
